enriched_description: A spiderlike arachnid with a small, compact, rounded to oval body that appears as a single fused unit with no visible waist separation between cephalothorax and abdomen. Possesses eight extremely long, slender legs that can exceed body length by a factor of 10 to 30, giving a spindly, delicate silhouette. Legs are thin and threadlike with fine segmentation visible under magnification. The body surface is smooth to granular with a leathery chitinous exoskeleton, typically colored in muted tones of brown, gray, or black. Lacks venom glands and silk-producing spinnerets. Two small eyes are positioned on a raised ocular tubercle (ocularium) near the anterior dorsal surface. The pedipalps are short and leg-like, used for sensing and manipulating food. Overall proportions are dominated by leg span, which can reach 5-10 cm while the body remains only 3-8 mm. The uniform body coloration and extraordinarily elongated legs distinguish it from true spiders, which have a clearly constricted waist (pedicel) between body segments.

An arachnid with a distinctly segmented body divided into a broad cephalothorax (prosoma) and a multi-segmented abdomen (opisthosoma). The cephalothorax bears a pair of large, robust pedipalp pincers (chelae) used for grasping prey, and four pairs of walking legs extending laterally. The abdomen is divided into a broad anterior mesosoma and a narrow, elongated, segmented metasoma (tail) that curves upward and forward over the dorsal surface, terminating in a bulbous venomous stinger (telson/aculeus). The exoskeleton is hard and chitinous with a glossy to matte finish, typically colored in earth tones of brown, black, yellow, or reddish-brown. The body exhibits bilateral symmetry with a flattened dorsoventral profile. The pincers vary in size relative to the body depending on species, ranging from slender to massively hypertrophied. The tail segments (metasomal segments) are clearly annulated, creating a ribbed, cylindrical appearance. Under ultraviolet light, the cuticle exhibits bright blue-green fluorescence due to beta-carboline and 7-hydroxy-4-methylcoumarin compounds in the exoskeleton. Body length ranges from 9 mm to over 20 cm. The combination of prominent pincers, segmented tail arching over the back, and the terminal stinger are diagnostic features distinguishing scorpions from other arachnids.

class_name: black and gold garden spider, Argiope aurantia
enriched_description: A large North American orb-weaving spider exhibiting striking sexual dimorphism, with females reaching 19-28 mm body length and males only 5-9 mm. The female cephalothorax is covered in dense silver-white hairs giving a frosted appearance. The abdomen is elongated and somewhat teardrop-shaped, displaying a bold pattern of black and bright yellow (gold) markings: a central black region flanked by paired yellow spots, with additional yellow bands along the lateral margins. The eight legs are long and banded with alternating black and yellow segments, with dark annulations at the joints. The spider constructs large, vertical orb webs (up to 60 cm diameter) featuring a distinctive stabilimentum—a conspicuous zigzag ribbon of dense white silk running vertically through the web center. The legs are held in four characteristic pairs when the spider rests at the web hub, forming an X-shaped posture. The abdomen has a slightly velvety texture due to dense setae coverage. Males are uniformly brown and significantly smaller, lacking the dramatic coloration. The black-and-yellow aposematic coloration, large body size, and signature zigzag web stabilimentum are key diagnostic markers distinguishing Argiope aurantia from other garden spiders.

A robust orb-weaving spider with a body length of 12-20 mm (females) and 7-11 mm (males). The cephalothorax is orange-tan to light brown with a darker central longitudinal stripe and radiating dark lines. The abdomen is large, globular to slightly pointed posteriorly, displaying a complex dorsal pattern of a central leaf-shaped or chevron-like marking in dark brown against a lighter orange-tan background, flanked by lateral dark bands. The eight legs are distinctly and darkly banded with alternating brown and pale annulations, creating a striped appearance. The legs are relatively thick and sturdy compared to many orb-weavers, with dense spination visible as fine bristle-like projections. The spider spins a new orb web nightly, typically 30-50 cm in diameter, often in sheltered locations such as barns, eaves, and porches. The ventral surface of the abdomen is lighter, often pale yellow or cream. The overall coloration provides cryptic camouflage against wooden surfaces and dried vegetation. The combination of orange-tan body coloration, darkly banded legs, leaf-patterned abdomen, and association with human structures distinguishes Araneus cavaticus from related orb-weaving species.

A European cross spider (orb-weaver) with a body length of 10-18 mm (females) and 5-9 mm (males). The most distinctive feature is a prominent white cross-shaped or cruciform pattern on the dorsal surface of the abdomen, formed by five or more white spots connected by white lines against a variable background of orange-brown, reddish-brown, or dark brown. The abdomen is globular and bulbous, significantly larger than the cephalothorax. The cephalothorax is covered in fine golden-brown hairs with a darker central region. The eight legs are banded with alternating dark brown and pale segments, and are covered with fine spines. The ventral side of the abdomen displays a silvery-white pattern with a central dark longitudinal stripe. The spider constructs large orb webs (up to 40 cm diameter) in gardens, hedgerows, and open woodland, typically positioned to catch flying insects. The white cross marking is highly variable in intensity but is consistently present, serving as the primary diagnostic feature. The overall body texture appears slightly velvety due to dense setae coverage. The cruciform abdominal marking, European distribution, and orb-web construction behavior distinguish Aranea diademata from other similarly sized orb-weaving spiders.

A venomous New World spider exhibiting extreme sexual dimorphism, with females reaching 8-14 mm body length and males only 3-4 mm. The female body is uniformly glossy black with a smooth, shiny exoskeleton that reflects light, giving a lacquered appearance. The abdomen is large, spherical to slightly ovoid, and bears the diagnostic bright red or orange hourglass-shaped marking on the ventral (underside) surface—two connected triangular patches that narrow at the center. Some females also display a row of smaller red or orange spots along the dorsal midline of the abdomen. The eight legs are long, slender, and uniformly black, lacking banding or patterning. The cephalothorax is smaller than the abdomen and also glossy black. Males are brown or gray with lighter abdominal markings and are not considered medically significant. Females build irregular, tangled cobwebs in sheltered locations (woodpiles, sheds, under rocks). The combination of glossy black coloration, spherical abdomen, thin unmarked legs, and the ventral red hourglass marking are definitive diagnostic features. The hourglass shape is complete and symmetrical in mature females, distinguishing Latrodectus mactans from other widow species which may have broken, partial, or differently colored markings.

A large, heavily built spider with a robust, densely hairy body. Body length ranges from 5 to 12 cm including legs, with some species exceeding 30 cm leg span. The entire body surface—cephalothorax, abdomen, and legs—is covered in dense, thick setae (hairs) ranging from short velvety pubescence to long bristle-like guard hairs, giving a fuzzy, plush texture. Coloration is predominantly earth-toned: dark brown, black, gray, or reddish-brown, with some species exhibiting iridescent blue, green, or pink hues on the legs or abdomen. The cephalothorax is broad and sturdy, bearing eight eyes arranged in two rows at the anterior margin. The chelicerae (fang-bearing mouthparts) are large, robust, and project downward, with prominent fangs visible from the front. The eight legs are thick, cylindrical, and heavily spined, with the first pair often elongated for sensory function. The abdomen is large, ovoid, and covered in dense hair; many New World species possess urticating (irritating) hairs on the dorsal abdomen that can be flicked as a defense mechanism. The overall silhouette is bulky and low-slung, with a wide stance. The combination of large size, dense hair coverage, robust build, prominent fangs, and ground-dwelling or burrowing habitat distinguishes tarantulas from all other spider families.

A robust, ground-dwelling hunting spider with a body length of 10-35 mm depending on species. The body is elongated and somewhat flattened dorsoventrally, adapted for rapid terrestrial locomotion. The cephalothorax is broad with a distinct central longitudinal stripe (light tan or cream) flanked by two darker lateral bands, creating a three-stripe pattern running the length of the carapace. The abdomen is elongated-oval with a variable mottled pattern of brown, gray, and black markings providing cryptic camouflage against soil, leaf litter, and bark. The eight legs are relatively long, sturdy, and covered with prominent spines; they are typically brown with darker annulations at the joints. The most distinctive anatomical feature is the eye arrangement: eight eyes in three rows—the anterior row has four small eyes, the middle row has two very large anterior median eyes that are highly reflective and give the spider a characteristic eyeshine, and the posterior row has two medium-sized eyes. The large median eyes are forward-facing, providing excellent binocular vision for active hunting. Wolf spiders do not build webs; they actively pursue prey on the ground. Females carry a spherical white egg sac attached to their spinnerets, and after hatching, the spiderlings ride on the mother's dorsal abdomen in a dense cluster. The combination of three-stripe carapace pattern, prominent forward-facing median eyes, ground-hunting behavior, and maternal egg-sac carrying behavior are diagnostic features.

A small parasitic arachnid with a dorsoventrally flattened, oval to teardrop-shaped body when unfed, becoming engorged, spherical, and greatly enlarged after blood feeding. Adult body length ranges from 2-3 mm unfed to 10-15 mm fully engorged. The body is divided into two regions: the anterior capitulum (mouthparts) and the posterior idiosoma (body). The capitulum bears a barbed hypostome (feeding tube) that projects anteriorly, flanked by a pair of segmented palps. The idiosoma is covered by a leathery, tough cuticle. In hard ticks (Ixodidae), a hard dorsal shield (scutum) covers the entire dorsal surface of males and the anterior portion of females; the scutum is often ornamented with colored enamel-like patterns in shades of brown, reddish-brown, or black. Soft ticks (Argasidae) lack a scutum and have a wrinkled, leathery integument. Adults possess eight legs (larvae have six), with the legs terminating in specialized adhesive structures (pulvilli) for host attachment. The body coloration is typically uniform brown, reddish-brown, or black, with some species displaying ornate white or silver markings on the scutum. The body surface is smooth to slightly textured, lacking the segmentation visible in insects. No antennae are present. The combination of flattened oval body shape, anterior mouthparts with barbed hypostome, eight legs in adults, leathery cuticle, and absence of antennae distinguish ticks from insects and other arachnids. The engorged state—where the body becomes a smooth, distended, grayish-blue sac—is a distinctive visual marker.

An elongated, dorsoventrally flattened arthropod with a body composed of numerous clearly defined segments (ranging from 15 to 173 segments depending on species), each bearing a single pair of legs extending laterally. Body length ranges from a few millimeters to over 30 cm in tropical species. The body exhibits bilateral symmetry with a distinct head bearing a pair of long, multi-segmented, threadlike antennae that extend forward and are constantly in motion. The head also bears a pair of large, prominent mandibles. The foremost body segment (behind the head) is modified: its leg pair is transformed into large, curved, venomous forcipules (modified prehensors) that project forward and inward, visible as prominent claw-like structures. The remaining body segments each bear one pair of walking legs, with legs increasing in length toward the posterior; the final pair of legs is often elongated and held backward, resembling antennae. The exoskeleton is smooth to slightly textured, with a glossy or matte finish, typically colored in shades of brown, reddish-brown, yellow, orange, or greenish. The dorsal surface of each segment may display darker longitudinal stripes or banding. The legs are slender, multi-segmented, and move in a characteristic wave-like undulating pattern during locomotion. The overall body profile is elongated and ribbon-like, with legs extending well beyond the body width, creating a fringed silhouette. The combination of flattened elongated body, one pair of legs per segment, venomous anterior forcipules, long antennae, and rapid undulating locomotion distinguish centipedes from millipedes (which have two pairs of legs per segment and a cylindrical body) and other arthropods.
